input.opening_narrative:
The morning is clear and cold. Twenty riders left Winterfell by the north gate before the sun was well up, and the road has climbed since then into the hills, where the snow lies in the shade of the rocks and the grass between is brown and stiff. The holdfast is a low stone tower with a wooden palisade, and the men who hold it have the deserter waiting inside the gate.

Lord Eddard rides at the head of the party on a tall grey. Jory Cassel and the guardsmen are around him. Robb is a little back, on the bay he favours, and Theon Greyjoy beside him with the long bundle of oiled cloth across his saddle that he has carried all the way from the castle. Jon's garron keeps its place by Bran's pony without being told; the pony is small and the boy on it sits very straight in his new wool cloak, his hands tight on the reins. He is seven. He has not seen this before.

The gate opens and two of the holdfast men bring the deserter out between them. He is not what a boy expects. He is old, with a grey stubble of beard, and his black cloak is torn and stained; he has lost an ear and part of a finger to frost, and the fingers of one hand are wrapped in a rag. His eyes go from face to face without settling on any. When he sees the grey horse and the man on it he stops walking, and the holdfast men have to move him.

Lord Eddard dismounts. He does not hurry. He pulls off his riding gloves and hands them to Jory, and Theon comes forward with the bundle and unwraps it, and the greatsword is there, broad as a hand and longer than Bran is tall, with the dark ripples in the steel that mark it as Valyrian. Theon holds it out across his arms. Lord Eddard takes it by the hilt.

The holdfast men have set a stump of ironwood in the yard, cut level. They walk the deserter to it. He goes down on his knees when they push him and puts his head on the wood himself, and one of them draws his hair aside so the neck is bare. He is saying something, low and fast, over and over. It is not a plea. The words are the same words each time and the men nearest him look at one another and do not answer.

Lord Eddard asks him his name and whether he knows the sentence. The old man says that he saw the white walkers, that they were there, that he was not lying. He says it to the stump. Lord Eddard says that a man of the Night's Watch who deserts his post forfeits his life, that he is sworn to give the king's justice, and that the sentence is death. He says it plainly, in the same voice he uses in his own hall, so that every man in the yard can hear it.

Robb has gone still on his horse. Theon is grinning, and stops when Jory looks at him. Bran's pony stamps and blows and the boy's hands on the reins do not move. Jon's garron stands close enough that the boy's stirrup is a hand's breadth from his own.

Lord Eddard sets his feet. He lifts Ice in both hands and the blade catches the light along its whole length, and the men who are standing too near the stump step back from it.

assumptions: Story-local calendar: Day 0 is the day of the execution in 298 AC; the party reaches the holdfast at about 08:00. The exact date is not established.

Ratings are inferences from what the novels show of Jon by this morning, not the television version: a well-trained boy of fourteen whose edge with a sword is Ser Rodrik's teaching rather than mastery, who rides and hunts, reads beyond his lessons, and has a bastard's habits of watching. No rating claims more than that record supports.
The four languages are the player's premise for this story, not book canon; the novels establish only the Common Tongue for Jon.
No later-book knowledge is preloaded: not the direwolves, not the raven from King's Landing, not the royal party, not his mother.
Money and counted stores are not established; he owns nothing counted.

character.aim: Ride with his father to the holdfast, see the deserter's sentence done, and keep Bran steady through it.
character.background: Jon was brought to Winterfell as an infant at the end of Robert's Rebellion and raised there by his father, Lord Eddard Stark, alongside the trueborn children of Eddard and Lady Catelyn. He does not know who his mother was; his father has never said. He has lived his whole life inside the castle and the country around it and has never seen the Wall, where his uncle Benjen serves, nor been south of the Neck. He shares Robb's lessons under Maester Luwin and Robb's practice yard under Ser Rodrik Cassel, with Theon Greyjoy, five years older, training beside them. Lady Catelyn has never wanted him at Winterfell and does not hide it. This morning he rides with his father, Robb, Theon and seven-year-old Bran to a holdfast in the hills where a deserter from the Night's Watch is to die by his father's hand.

character.name: Jon Snow

appearance.Distinguishing features: The long solemn face of the Starks; of the children at Winterfell he looks most like his father. Slender where Robb is muscular, dark where Robb is fair, graceful and quick where Robb is strong and fast.
appearance.Eyes: Grey so dark they look black.
appearance.Height/build: Lean and not yet at his full height.

background_details.Arms: Ser Rodrik has had Jon in the yard since he could hold a wooden sword. He drills with Robb daily and with Theon often; the master-at-arms rates him well, and in the yard he and Robb are an even match, Jon quick and graceful where Robb is strong and fast. His edge is a good teacher's training, not any mastery: against boys who never had one he looks better than he is. He has learned footwork, guards, the cuts and the recovery, and to fight with a shield on his arm, all against boys and against the master-at-arms who is teaching him. He has never fought in armor heavier than a padded jack and mail shirt, never in a line, never against a man who wanted him dead. He wrestles well enough for his weight. He has shot a bow since he was small and can hit a target; Theon is the better archer by a wide margin and says so.
background_details.Conduct at Winterfell: He knows how a great hall is ordered, where he may sit and where he may not, how to serve at table and when to be silent. He can speak to a lord's son as an equal and to a servant as a lord's son should. He has no experience of court beyond his father's hall.
background_details.Letters and lessons: Maester Luwin taught him to read and write a fair hand, to reckon, and to know the great houses, their arms, their seats and their words. He read more than the lessons required: the Kings of Winter and the Long Night as the maester tells them and as Old Nan tells them, which is not the same; the First Men; the Free Cities; the Young Dragon's conquest of Dorne, which he knows nearly by heart. He has had the lessons in law and custom that a lord's son gets, and knows that as a bastard none of it is his. His tongues are the one thing in his schooling that goes beyond a lord's son's: the Old Tongue of the First Men, High Valyrian from the maester's books, and the Low Valyrian of the Free Cities, each of which he speaks, reads and writes as readily as the Common Tongue.
background_details.Riding and the wild: Jon has ridden since he was a small boy and sits a horse well, on the road and at speed. He has hunted with his father's party in the wolfswood and knows its near paths, how a deer moves, where the game trails run, and how to set a snare. He can make a fire and sleep rough for a night or two in summer weather. He has never crossed unknown country on his own, never navigated by more than a known road, and knows the true North beyond the wolfswood only from stories.
background_details.The old gods: He keeps the old gods with his father, before the heart tree in the godswood. He knows the customs, the oaths sworn there, and the stories; there is nothing more to know.
background_details.Watching: A bastard in a lady's household learns to notice. Jon is markedly observant: he reads a room and the people in it before he speaks, keeps his own counsel, and knows when he is being mocked before the sentence ends. He does not lie well and does not care to, but he can keep a thing to himself for years.

disposition.Conduct: He keeps his word and expects his father's word to be kept. He does not start a fight but does not walk away from one. He minds a slight and does not show it, and broods on his bastardy more than he lets anyone see. He is protective of Arya and of Bran and defers to Robb without resenting him. He wants a place that is his by his own doing, and has begun to think that place is the Wall.
disposition.Manner: He speaks plainly, listens more than he talks, watches before he acts, and judges quickly.
disposition.Temper and pride: He is a lord's son in everything but name and does not yet know how much that has given him; he can be quick to think others hate him for being better when they hate him for thinking so. Pressed on his bastardy or told to wait, his temper shows, and he says the sharp thing before the careful one.
disposition.Wit: Dry and sardonic, kept for Robb and Arya and for anyone who earns it; more often a thought than a spoken line.

Benjen Stark: uncle, First Ranger; visits Winterfell now and then and is kind to him; the reason the Wall has a face.

character.background: Jon was brought to Winterfell as an infant at the end of Robert's Rebellion and raised there by his father, Lord Eddard Stark, alongside the trueborn children of Eddard and Lady Catelyn. He does not know who his mother was; his father has never said. He has lived his whole life inside the castle and the country around it and has never seen the Wall, where his uncle Benjen serves, nor been south of the Neck. He shares Robb's lessons under Maester Luwin and Robb's practice yard under Ser Rodrik Cassel, with Theon Greyjoy, five years older, training beside them. Lady Catelyn has never wanted him at Winterfell and does not hide it. This morning he rides with his father, Robb, Theon and seven-year-old Bran to a holdfast in the hills where a deserter from the Night's Watch is to die by his father's hand.

character.name: Jon Snow

appearance.Distinguishing features: The long solemn face of the Starks; of the children at Winterfell he looks most like his father. Slender where Robb is muscular, dark where Robb is fair, graceful and quick where Robb is strong and fast.
appearance.Eyes: Grey so dark they look black.
appearance.Height/build: Lean and not yet at his full height.

background_details.Arms: Ser Rodrik has had Jon in the yard since he could hold a wooden sword. He drills with Robb daily and with Theon often; the master-at-arms rates him well, and in the yard he and Robb are an even match, Jon quick and graceful where Robb is strong and fast. His edge is a good teacher's training, not any mastery: against boys who never had one he looks better than he is. He has learned footwork, guards, the cuts and the recovery, and to fight with a shield on his arm, all against boys and against the master-at-arms who is teaching him. He has never fought in armor heavier than a padded jack and mail shirt, never in a line, never against a man who wanted him dead. He wrestles well enough for his weight. He has shot a bow since he was small and can hit a target; Theon is the better archer by a wide margin and says so.
background_details.Conduct at Winterfell: He knows how a great hall is ordered, where he may sit and where he may not, how to serve at table and when to be silent. He can speak to a lord's son as an equal and to a servant as a lord's son should. He has no experience of court beyond his father's hall.
background_details.Letters and lessons: Maester Luwin taught him to read and write a fair hand, to reckon, and to know the great houses, their arms, their seats and their words. He read more than the lessons required: the Kings of Winter and the Long Night as the maester tells them and as Old Nan tells them, which is not the same; the First Men; the Free Cities; the Young Dragon's conquest of Dorne, which he knows nearly by heart. He has had the lessons in law and custom that a lord's son gets, and knows that as a bastard none of it is his. His tongues are the one thing in his schooling that goes beyond a lord's son's: the Old Tongue of the First Men, High Valyrian from the maester's books, and the Low Valyrian of the Free Cities, each of which he speaks, reads and writes as readily as the Common Tongue.
background_details.Riding and the wild: Jon has ridden since he was a small boy and sits a horse well, on the road and at speed. He has hunted with his father's party in the wolfswood and knows its near paths, how a deer moves, where the game trails run, and how to set a snare. He can make a fire and sleep rough for a night or two in summer weather. He has never crossed unknown country on his own, never navigated by more than a known road, and knows the true North beyond the wolfswood only from stories.
background_details.The old gods: He keeps the old gods with his father, before the heart tree in the godswood. He knows the customs, the oaths sworn there, and the stories; there is nothing more to know.
background_details.Watching: A bastard in a lady's household learns to notice. Jon is markedly observant: he reads a room and the people in it before he speaks, keeps his own counsel, and knows when he is being mocked before the sentence ends. He does not lie well and does not care to, but he can keep a thing to himself for years.

disposition.Conduct: He keeps his word and expects his father's word to be kept. He does not start a fight but does not walk away from one. He minds a slight and does not show it, and broods on his bastardy more than he lets anyone see. He is protective of Arya and of Bran and defers to Robb without resenting him. He wants a place that is his by his own doing, and has begun to think that place is the Wall.
disposition.Manner: He speaks plainly, listens more than he talks, watches before he acts, and judges quickly.
disposition.Temper and pride: He is a lord's son in everything but name and does not yet know how much that has given him; he can be quick to think others hate him for being better when they hate him for thinking so. Pressed on his bastardy or told to wait, his temper shows, and he says the sharp thing before the careful one.
disposition.Wit: Dry and sardonic, kept for Robb and Arya and for anyone who earns it; more often a thought than a spoken line.

knowledge: It is the ninth year of a long summer, 298 AC. Robert Baratheon is king; Jon Arryn is his Hand, so far as Winterfell has heard.
A deserter from the Night's Watch was taken near a holdfast in the hills and is to die this morning by his father's hand.
His uncle Benjen is at the Wall. The Watch takes bastards and lets them rise.
His mother's name and fate are unknown to him; his father will not speak of her.
Old Nan's stories of the Others and the Long Night; the maester's histories, which treat them as stories.
The deserter, kneeling at the block, says he saw the white walkers and was not lying.
